tldr: For quadrupedal robots using depth cameras, the authors proposed "REDACT," a framework that maintains robust traversal even under unmodeled visual drops, noise, and distractors, using local feature agreement checks and calibration based solely on clean data.
hero_caption: Zero-shot real-world traversal experiments with REDACT in environments with unseen visual disturbances. The robot reliably clears obstacles even with unmodeled cardboard pillars placed right next to hurdles, fallen logs and distracting trees in a forest, and severe depth dropouts caused by undergrowth and dead leaves.
overview:
In recent years, quadrupedal robot locomotion leveraging depth images and deep reinforcement learning has drawn major attention for agile parkour maneuvers and rough-terrain traversal. However, in forests and complex outdoor environments, unpredictable visual noise often occurs—such as occlusions from hanging foliage, sensor noise from weather and sunlight, and extraneous objects near the path—which simulators cannot fully capture during training. With conventional methods, these out-of-distribution inputs corrupt visual features, putting robots at risk of steering off course or falling over.

To tackle this, instead of relying on data augmentation tailored to specific anticipated noise, the authors proposed REDACT (Retaining Evidence Despite Artifacts for Continued Traversal), a framework that handles unseen noise through model architecture and gating. Specifically, using a resilient residual-network visual encoder, REDACT introduces "consensus gating": each spatial cell (local patch) in the feature map predicts the overall scene representation, and discordant abnormal cells are automatically detected and excluded from pooling. The threshold for filtering is determined via conformal calibration using only clean simulation data, requiring no prior knowledge of the corruption types.

In evaluation experiments across highly challenging simulation scenarios with unseen noise, occlusions, and side distractors, REDACT significantly outperformed conventional parkour baselines in traversal success. Furthermore, in zero-shot transfer trials on a commercial quadruped robot (Unitree Go2), the robot conquered fallen logs in a natural forest with severe depth dropouts caused by sunlight and undergrowth, continuing to traverse without falling.
contributions: Proposed REDACT, a teacher-student reinforcement learning framework that preserves useful terrain evidence to maintain agile locomotion under unseen visual noise and occlusions.
Developed a consensus-gating mechanism that filters out corrupted local features based on prediction agreement (consensus) across feature map cells.
Enabled setting the consensus-gating rejection threshold via conformal calibration using only clean observation data, without needing corrupted images.

Demonstrated substantial performance gains over existing baselines across diverse unseen simulation corruptions, and validated zero-shot transfer to real-world forest environments without additional training.

sections.heading: Venturing into Forests and Unseen Environments: Why Visual Locomotion Is Fragile to Noise
sections.summary: In rough terrains and forests, vision is vital for agile locomotion, yet occlusions from foliage and sensor noise often introduce out-of-distribution depth inputs. This paper introduces REDACT, combining an improved visual encoder with local consensus-based feature filtering to handle unmodeled noise.
sections.details:
Unstructured outdoor settings like forests present countless hazards that impede legged robots, including tree roots, fallen logs, undergrowth, and steep elevation changes. Overcoming these through jumping or climbing requires vision to read the terrain before contact.

Recently, deep reinforcement learning combining proprioception (internal states like joint positions and velocities) with depth camera inputs has unlocked impressive parkour behaviors. However, these methods largely assume clean depth images like those seen in simulation. In real forests, robots encounter visual noise (out-of-distribution data) that simulators rarely cover exhaustively, such as occlusions from hanging vines and leaves, range-measurement dropouts caused by weather or direct sunlight, and standing trees alongside the travel path.

When a visual encoder outputs corrupted features due to unseen noise, the entire control policy can be derailed, leading to abrupt turning or falls. While synthetic data augmentation is widely used, it cannot guarantee robustness against corruption types omitted from training. Therefore, this study presents REDACT, a framework that assumes no prior knowledge of corruptions, autonomously removes corrupted feature regions at runtime, and keeps walking using only the remaining clean evidence.

sections.heading: Handling Blind or Corrupted Vision: Prior Limitations and Key Insights
sections.summary: Previous works either fell back to proprioception and memory when vision was disrupted or gated the entire image, struggling to salvage partial visual cues. REDACT draws inspiration from robust deep residual architectures and localized occlusion defenses in image classification, adapting them to locomotion.
sections.details:
### Visual Gating and Fallback Behaviors
Several approaches have explored what to do when vision becomes untrustworthy. For example, some methods drop vision entirely and rely purely on proprioception or short-term memory once depth reconstruction error flags corrupt vision. However, discarding the whole image because of a few vines or patches of noise also discards valuable information about the obstacles directly ahead. Other works sample terrain heights and weight them by confidence, but handling diverse, unmodeled degradations on egocentric depth images directly from an onboard camera has remained an open challenge.

### Robust Feature Aggregation and Visual Encoders
In adversarial image recognition, defenses like PatchGuard constrain the feature extractor's receptive field to mask suspicious regions even when localized noise patches are inserted. However, sensor noise and occlusions on legged robots are not always confined to neat local patches; they can scatter across the image, making the extent of noise hard to define beforehand.

Additionally, visual locomotion policies traditionally rely on very shallow convolutional neural networks (ConvNets) to reduce computational latency (Fig. F2 left). But shallow networks easily propagate noise-induced feature distortions directly to downstream controllers. This work adopts an IMPALA-style deep residual architecture with Group Normalization, proven in reinforcement learning, to significantly boost the baseline resilience of the encoder itself.

captions.F2: Comparison between the shallow ConvNet standard in parkour baselines (left, ~8M parameters) and the residual encoder adopted in REDACT (right, ~1.5M parameters). REDACT reduces parameter count by roughly 5x while introducing deep residual blocks and Group Normalization (GN) to suppress feature blowups.

sections.heading: How REDACT Works: Filtering Noise via Consensus and Clean Calibration
sections.summary: Building on a teacher-student framework with privileged training, REDACT introduces a residual encoder, persistent masking, and a consensus gate that checks agreement across feature cells. Each cell predicts the pooled latent state, and cells deviating from the median prediction are automatically pruned.
sections.details:
### III-A Teacher Policy Training
Training begins with a teacher policy that accesses privileged simulation data (accurate local terrain scans and exact physical robot states) (Fig. F3 (a)). To capture multiple critical zones simultaneously—such as takeoff and landing spots—the teacher uses a multi-query cross-attention mechanism. Furthermore, training incorporates entropy regularization to avoid diffuse attention, an overlap penalty to prevent distinct queries from focusing on identical locations, and temporal smoothness regularization on latents. This produces a well-structured terrain representation that is easier for the student network to distill from camera inputs.

### III-B Student Policy Training
The student network receives onboard depth camera images instead of privileged point clouds (Fig. F3 (b)). The encoder maps the input into a $4\times 6$ grid of 24 spatial feature cells $f_\ell$ (Fig. F2 right).

Crucially, REDACT attaches a linear head to each cell to predict the pooled whole-image latent representation (the pooled latent over all cells). On clean images, every cell should be able to predict the overall scene context with reasonable consistency. During training, the pooled latent with a stop-gradient acts as the teacher target for these cell heads.

To ensure the policy remains stable when cells are dropped by gating or obscured by noise, persistent feature masking (similar to DropBlock and random cell masking) is applied during training. Additionally, features pass through Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ), preventing minor feature fluctuations from disrupting the downstream GRU (recurrent neural network).

### III-C Conformal Calibration and Deployment
At deployment, the system computes the Euclidean distance between each cell's prediction $\hat{u}_\ell$ and the leave-one-out (LOO) median of predictions from all other cells as a disagreement score (Eq. 8). If a local region suffers from noise or occlusion, its prediction diverges sharply from the others, causing its disagreement score to spike.

To determine what counts as an anomaly, the method borrows conformal calibration from uncertainty estimation. Using roughly 3,500 clean rollout episodes in simulation without any corrupted images, REDACT calculates the 99th percentile of disagreement scores offline for each cell location to set cell-specific thresholds $\tau_\ell$ (Eq. 9).

During traversal, cells exceeding their threshold are excluded from average pooling, and the policy controls the robot using the latent built only from the surviving clean cells (Fig. F3 (c)). If 18 or more cells are flagged, a fallback safety rule retains all but the worst 6 discordant cells to prevent extreme information starvation.

captions.F3: Overall REDACT pipeline. (a) Teacher training capturing terrain via multi-query cross-attention from privileged scans; (b) Student training using local cell-level whole-latent prediction and persistent masking; (c) Deployment using the consensus gate with thresholds calibrated on clean data to filter abnormal cells.
captions.F5: The four terrain types used in simulation evaluation (left: slope ramps, crevasses, hurdles, stairs) and examples of visual corruptions applied at test time (right). Degradations cover flying pixels, Gaussian noise, Perlin dropout, hanging vine occlusions, and off-path distractor pillars.

sections.heading: Unstopped by Unseen Visual Noise: Simulation and Real-World Validation
sections.summary: Under unseen corruptions in simulation, REDACT achieved traversal success rates far superior to baseline methods and augmentation models. In real-world Unitree Go2 experiments, it demonstrated zero-shot traversal across hurdles with side distractors and fallen logs in natural forests.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Baseline Comparisons
Experiments compared REDACT against state-of-the-art parkour baselines like Extreme Parkour and REAL using the Unitree Go2 quadruped. On clean terrain, all methods achieve high success rates. However, introducing unmodeled depth corruptions (Gaussian noise, flying pixels, Perlin dropout, vine occlusions) or off-path distractor pillars (pillar hurdles) revealed massive performance gaps. Distractor pillars sit next to hurdles without blocking the route, yet baselines steered off course or misstepped and fell. In contrast, REDACT disregarded the visual distractors and maintained high success.

### IV-C Generalization to Unseen Corruptions and Limits of Augmentation
Addressing whether data augmentation alone suffices, the authors trained conventional ConvNet baselines with specific corruptions (e.g., Gaussian noise or vine occlusions) and evaluated them on unmodeled noise types. A ConvNet trained on vine occlusions collapsed under Gaussian noise and flying pixels (dropping to 1.9% success on flying pixels), highlighting the limits of synthetic augmentation. Under the most severe tier of unseen corruptions, augmented baselines averaged only 37% success, whereas REDACT without any depth augmentation reached 74%.

### IV-D & IV-E Ablations and Gate Behavior Analysis
Ablation studies showed that the residual architecture and Group Normalization elevated baseline resilience, while consensus gating delivered drastic gains against localized occlusions and distractors (success under vine occlusions rose from 39.0% without gating to 65.7% with gating). As shown in Fig. F8, visualizing latents through a depth reconstruction decoder reveals that cells obscured by vines are cleanly flagged and excluded, preserving reconstructed depth images nearly identical to clean inputs.

### IV-F Real-World Zero-Shot Traversal
Policies trained entirely in simulation were deployed zero-shot to a physical Go2 equipped with an onboard Jetson Orin Nano. When an unmodeled cardboard pillar was placed next to a hurdle, the baseline was drawn toward the pillar and crashed, while REDACT moved straight ahead and leaped over the hurdle unaffected. Furthermore, in a natural forest (Fig. F9) with dense dead leaves, branches, fallen logs, and severe sunlight dropouts, REDACT cleared fallen logs in 7 out of 10 trials. Proprioception and vision cooperated smoothly to recover from foot slips on bark and roots, sustaining uninterrupted traversal.

captions.F8: Feature reconstruction decoding under vine occlusions. Cells where occlusions occur (flagged cells, far right) are cleanly rejected by the gate. The decoded depth from gated latents (decode gated) stays remarkably close to reconstructions from clean depth inputs.
captions.F9: Physical Go2 traversing fallen logs in a natural forest. As seen in the onboard depth images (bottom), despite widespread black dropout regions from sunlight and heavy background clutter from undergrowth and branches, the robot stabilizes its posture and climbs over the logs.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Advancing Visual Robustness through Architecture and Algorithms
sections.summary: REDACT is an effective framework that preserves vital terrain information for continuous locomotion under unseen visual degradation. Combining a residual encoder, persistent masking, consensus gating, and clean-data conformal calibration marks a major step forward for real-world rough-terrain traversal.
sections.details:
This paper presented REDACT, a framework that safeguards robot locomotion against unseen visual noise and occlusions that synthetic data augmentation cannot fully cover.

While visual locomotion policies traditionally favor shallow convolutional networks for lightweight execution, properly configuring residual connections and Group Normalization dramatically boosts corruption resistance while keeping computational load modest. Moreover, having spatial cells predict the global context to detect disagreements via consensus gating, paired with conformal calibration using clean data alone, offers an elegant defense requiring zero prior knowledge of corruption types.

Rigorous simulation benchmarks and real-world forest trials demonstrate that REDACT provides a powerful, practical solution for autonomous mobile robots heading into unfamiliar environments.

takeaways: Relying solely on image data augmentation (domain randomization) has fundamental limits and struggles to generalize to unseen corruption families.
Having each feature map cell predict the whole-image latent and checking its divergence from the median provides accurate, unsupervised detection and removal of unknown local noise and occlusions.
Conformal calibration using percentiles derived purely from clean observation data offers an effective, lightweight way to set anomaly thresholds without corruption examples.
Replacing shallow CNN encoders with GroupNorm-equipped residual networks (IMPALA-style) substantially enhances the baseline visual robustness of locomotion policies.
limitations: Consensus gating struggles to detect high-frequency, uniform full-image noise (such as fine Gaussian noise) because all cells shift similarly, though the encoder's innate resilience helps compensate.
When over 18 cells are flagged and the fallback triggers (dropping only the worst 6 cells), some corrupted features exceeding the threshold can still enter pooling.

Onboard depth inference latency with gating is 8.8 ms (matching a ~10 Hz camera update rate), which may require further computational optimization for extreme high-speed parkour needing higher control frequencies.
